title: Manzanita Cycles 32” Gravel Bike Review: Analog Advancement – Paul Kalifatidi
content:
There is a lot of hype and a lot of vitriol surrounding 32″ wheels. We hope this calmer take on the platform helps smooth out some of the aggressive opinions on the subject in the same way it helps smooth out the rough stuff flying under these big hoops. Paul has been riding this Manzanita Cycles 32er gravel bike – commissioned by Charles Wells of Verum Velo – for the past two months and has formed his opinions on the subject.

My Blender

I have a favorite kale pesto recipe that a roommate taught me. It’s quick, easily altered, and ticks all the boxes. This is a crazy way to start off a bike review, but hear me out: we are going to start with a review of my blender. And yes, I’ll give you the recipe.

My blender is a NutriBullet NB-101S. It’s not their top-of-the-line model, as it only has two modes, minimal accessories, and costs less than $70. Frankly, I love that it doesn’t have any modes, as my four jobs and the current state of the economy has me up to my neck in decision fatigue. I used to have a roommate with a Vitamix, and I would frequently find myself staring at all the knobs, buttons, and dials just trying to figure out which concerto I needed to play to achieve my sauce.

Screw that.

I have no such issues with my NutriBullet NB-101s. I put my kale, basil, garlic, parmesan, salt, apple cider vinegar, olive oil, and pasta water into the container, I screw the blades on, and I push the whole assembly into the blender. I can walk away for a minute and come back to buttery smooth pesto. It’s awesome.

And here’s why I start this incredibly serious bike review with my blender: the NutriBullet, much like the Manzanita, has basically zero features or moving parts, and yet, produces the smoothest product ever. Let’s get into bikes.

Why 32″?

The whole premise behind the larger tire size is increased rollover. This means that it requires less energy to pull or push the wheel up and over obstacles. When descending, you have speed on your side. When climbing, there is more responsibility on the rider to get the wheels up and over obstacles. On the Manzanita, I noticed it was easier to maintain speed. The terrain required less energy to roll across. Dips didn’t feel like they sucked the bike down, and bumps didn’t seem to throw it off as much. Could you still feel those features? Of course. This is a bicycle, not a magic carpet, no matter how much some people might try to convince you.

I also noticed an increased amount of traction. The larger wheel makes a larger contact patch on the ground. The best way I can describe it is going up one level of knobby from what you would expect to feel. For example, I imagine it felt more like riding a Teravail Rutland than a Teravail Cannonball, even though I was technically riding the Cannonball tread pattern. It’s impossible to say as I didn’t have a knobbier tire of the same size, but that’s what I think it would have felt like.

29″ vs. 32″ Frame Differences

There are a few key differences between 29″ and 32″ wheeled frames that extend beyond just angles. Let’s quickly go over them.

Headtube: the headtube of 32″ wheeled bikes is shorter to accommodate the wider wheels and associated longer forks; this makes for a packaging conundrum on smaller frame sizes as steel headtubes are not commonly made less than 95 mm in length. Any shorter, and there’ll be no room to join the top tube and down tube to the head tube in a strong enough fashion.

Hub Spacing: a large part of the 32″ wheel debate has been around hub spacing. Wider wheels need longer spokes, which makes for a more flexy wheel. To achieve a wheel with the desired stiffness characteristics, most framebuilders are speccing Boost hubs more commonly used on mountain bikes. The Manzanita features Boost spacing both front and rear.

Forks: the fork blades must be 1.5″ longer (at minimum) to accommodate the wider wheel. There are still no carbon forks available to framebuilders explicitly built for the 32″ wheel. This means that most framebuilders are using suspension-corrected rigid mountain bike forks that feature longer axle-to-crown lengths and Boost spacing. Like many 32″ bikes that I have seen, the Manzanita uses the Enve Composites mountain fork.

Frame: obviously, the frame is going to have some sizable differences in comparison to bikes to which you are accustomed. The seatstays and chainstays must be longer, and the seat tube needs to show off its yoga ability to get out of the way. Bottom brackets are lower. Downtubes will have a harder time clearing the front tire, especially if the fork’s axle-to-crown is tucked as close to the tire as possible. Simply put: fitting giant hoops is hard.

Geometry

I am not a geometry whiz. I can look at a geometry chart and infer how a bike will ride, but I also know that I can get used to just about anything. In the past year, I have spent a lot of time on 6 different bikes – three gravel bikes and three mountain bikes. They all have different geometry, they all handle differently, and I have figured out how to ride all of them. Where one geometry might be at a disadvantage, another might shine.

My hot take, perhaps even Dust Up worthy, is that we spend too much time debating tiny numbers and differences. The bike is a rigid object; its measurements are more or less set in stone once the tubes are mitered and tacked. Yes, we can adjust the fit with changes to the handlebars, stem, saddle position, and crank lengths, but those don’t affect the handling as much as they do our own comfort. Our bodies are large moldable sacks of water – with a bit of a bend of the elbow, and most importantly, a malleable mind, it can be quite easy to adapt to a myriad of geometries.

The goal of this project was to create a well-rounded gravel bike. Sure, you can race it. Yes, you can ride chunky singletrack. But the perfect venue and terrain would be a pleasant long route on mixed surfaces with sufficient chunk to question “gravel” as a descriptor. The riding position is not narrow and tucked. With this bike, the speed comes from the confidence to entertain it and the capability to maintain it.

When debating geometry and parts, we discussed if this bike should try to feel like something familiar, like a 69º head tube angle on a 29″ wheeled bike. This would closely match many drop-bar 29ers like the Salsa Cutthroat and my own Northern Frameworks. While on paper, matching that trail and handling seems doable, the actual result is not the same. Nick from Manzanita weighed in with his opinion:

“The weight of the front wheel has more impact on how a bike handles than the head tube angle or trail. I learned this when I made my ultralight hardtail a few years ago. Even with a slack 66º HTA for an XC bike, the front wheel was so light that the bike felt like riding a road bike. Very responsive. If I switched to a more normally weighted front wheel, the bike handled like a standard XC mountain bike.

There’s no getting around that 32” wheels are going to be heavier than what people are used to with 29ers. Additionally, the long chainstays move more weight to the front wheel. You can’t design the bike to handle like a 29er. Even if you were able to make the headtube angle and trail the same as my Whippet for instance, the bike is still going to feel more planted.

I didn’t worry about making the bike handle like something I’m familiar with. I let the 32” wheels be 32” wheels. I made the chainstays as short as possible to test my fabrication skills and designed the front end to be as short as possible but not so short that the rider should experience toe overlap.

My initial opinion of the bike after a 1-hour ride on some flat dirt roads and hilly paved roads was that the bike handled great. Yes, the front end feels more planted or “sluggish”, although I hate that term because of its negative connotations. But that planted feeling meant cornering was off the charts good. I could really lean the bike and let it rip.”

I agree with Nick. The steering isn’t as quick-feeling as most gravel bikes, but it’s still lighter-feeling than a mountain bike.

The rear of the bike was not as long as I expected. I had been riding this bike for several weeks before I ever took a look at the geo chart, which I finally did after a funny moment. For some reason, I had not yet tried to wheelie the bike. I imagined that it would take effort to stand the bike on the rear tire, given the large wheel size and expected long rear-center. I pulled hard… and just about back flipped. This bike stood up with no effort and was a pleasure to keep there. I texted Nick about the rear center as soon as the front wheel touched the ground. It was only 427 mm – shorter than any mountain bike I had in the fleet. I was impressed.

Frame Details

Nick can make a bike; that much is clear. When I lifted this bike out of the box, I was blown away by how light it was. It felt more like lifting a carbon gravel bike. Given its svelte tubeset, the frame is quite flexy. I don’t mind a noodle-like frame, but I wouldn’t even have described the Manzanita as such. There were plenty of supporting characters in the pleasant riding experience.

Some of my favorite details were the 3D-printed brake cable guides on the underside of the chainstay. Otherwise, this bike was pleasantly simple: no headset cable routing, no sliding dropouts, and no bullshit.

The Build

This bike was commissioned by Charles Wells, the owner of Verum Wheels. Charles and I met at last year’s MADE. We are about the same size, so Charles had an idea. He wanted to release 32″ wheels, and I wanted to try them. So we collaborated on this project along with Nick Jensen from Manzanita Cycles and his frame building expertise. Charles’ whole goal was to provide the highest-quality wheels to better evaluate the 32er platform. Bad wheels make a huge difference, so knowing that the wheels are not taking away from the riding experience gave me faith that the sensations I felt were true.

That said, I do think that being on 32″ wheels laced to Berd spokes, known for their vibration-absorbing ride quality, coupled with the flexy steel frame, played a role in making the smoothest bike I had ever ridden.

Charles spared few expenses when it came to speccing the Manzanita. The three of us discussed the parts spec and agreed that wider handlebars were the way to go, given the short stem length. I was quite familiar with the 48 cm Gravel Bars as I have a set on my personal bike which seeks a similar terrain and riding style. I had not yet ridden a mullet Shimano GRX/XTR drivetrain, but, to nobody’s surprise, I was pleased with the ergonomics and speedy shifting. I played around with stem length and seatpost offset, which we will discuss towards the end of the article.

Verum x30 32″

When 29″ wheels came onto the market, bike design went through growing pains. Thru-axles still weren’t the ubiquitous standard, and most hubs were 142 mm in width. Wheel compliance, or rather too much compliance, became an issue due to the increased wheel width and decreased wheel rigidity. An easy solution is to increase the distance between the hub flanges, which creates a better bracing angle for the spokes. This same debate is currently happening with 32″ wheels. Do 32″ gravel bikes need to have Boost 148 mm and 110 mm hubs? Do 32″ mountain bikes need Super Boost hubs? Logic would say that the same changes that were made when going from 27.5″ wheels to 29″ wheels would need to be entertained for this new wheel size.

The Manzanita uses Boost hub spacing front and rear. Charles built these Verum x30 wheels using Berd Polylight Spokes and Erase Components hubs that feature hooked flanges per Berd’s Equal Spoke Length (ESL) specification. The rims themselves are Charles’ own design and feature an asymmetric profile to better brace the spokes. Most notably, all Verum wheels feature no spoke holes on the rim bed. Therefore, there is also no need for rim tape. I have an upcoming review dedicated to a set of Verum wheels where I’ll discuss this at length. For now, know that the advantages of such a system are mostly in the elimination of any rim tape leaks or errors and less of a chance that sealant makes its way into the rim. Yes, it takes a bit longer to build, but the results are seemingly worth the 20 minutes of nipple maneuvering.

Oh, and these wheels were stupid light.

This bike shipped to me with Maxxis Aspen 32″ x 2.4″ tires that were the only tires available at the time. I never ended up riding them; Teravail was able to send me 2.2″ Cannonballs before they were released. I never ran the 2.4″ tires because of the small amount of toe overlap I experienced. Given that I was going to be riding this bike on a lot of singletrack, and frequently in places where overlapping tires and toes can have very steep consequences, I opted to skip such an experience. I experienced no toe overlap with the 2.2″ tires, 170 mm cranks, and my size ~43 shoes. While you might chastise me for not riding the larger tire out of curiosity, I will fire back and say that I know it wouldn’t have completely altered the experience.

Small Box vs Large Box

In rock climbing, there is a rough measurement or descriptor that we call “box.” It is easy to conceptualize: spread your arms and legs out as wide as they will go, Vitruvian Man style, and that is your box. Large humans have a “large box” and small humans have a “small box.” We can also describe individual climbing moves, sequences, and boulder problems as being “small box” or “big box.”

If you have one of those black-and-yellow plastic boxes that are seemingly ubiquitous in the garages and gear closets of outdoor-minded folk, I invite you to go try to stuff yourself inside. Now, ask someone of a different size to do the same. Notice a difference? Stuffing yourself inside that container is a “small box” kind of move. A smaller human is going to do better. Likewise, trying to touch all of the walls inside a wheelchair-accessible Porta-potty would be considered a “big box” move.

32″ wheels are “big box” in that they are going to work better for larger riders. Or, if you don’t care about how your bike looks, it might work for medium-sized riders, and even small-sized riders (if the bike exists). I am 5’10” and think I’m on the cusp of being too small for this wheel size. I also don’t want to ride an ugly bike no matter how nice it might ride. I enjoy bicycles for more than how they ride. Forever, I think I’ll lean on my late Grandfather for this opinion. He was a wooden boat builder. Wooden boats are not the lightest, they’re not the highest performing, and they’re not the most durable. However, they have so much soul and beauty, and that is why we love them.

I also have a theory: wheel size does affect the capability of a bike, but so does center of mass. A really tall rider has a significantly higher center of mass than a really short rider. As a wheel climbs over an obstacle, it has to work against the leverage of that center of mass. If the center of mass is closer to the ground, there is less leverage on that wheel, and it moves more easily. This is quite noticeable on a mountain bike flying through roots or rocks. Stand high over the bike, and the suspension seems to get flustered. Sit really low, and things move smoother.

A large part of the discourse surrounding these giant hoops is how they don’t fit well for smaller riders. From a framebuilding standpoint, fitting these large hoops into a small frame is an engineering challenge. Even if the wheels fit, the rider might not fit the frame. Toe overlap, butt-to-tire clearance, and excessive stack height are the most likely issues that small riders might face.

While initially I fully agreed with this, I now question whether 32″ is wrong for “small box” folks. Salsa makes the Fargo in a 32″ variant, and they have a full size run all the way down to a size small meant to fit someone as short as 5’2″. A 5’3″ woman was part of the development and she loves the capability of the platform. So who am I to judge?

I think there is an over-reaction to 32″ bikes within the world of bike media and a lot of it seems to be driven by divisive algorithm metrics. While I understand the need for publications and journalists to make a living, I don’t want to participate in the vitriol and excessive hype that I’ve been seeing. I have no issues with 32″ wheels, even though I will likely never choose to purchase them. Here’s why: we have always chosen bikes for a huge variety of reasons: aesthetics, ride quality, intent, and most importantly, vibes.

Initial Impressions

My first time pedaling a 32″ bike was outside of Ornot when Daniel Yang brought his Neuhaus Metalworks Hummingbird for people to take a look at. Immediately, I noticed that the bike did not react quite as much when it hit small curbs and bumps and felt a bit resistant to leaning over. Besides that, there wasn’t anything jaw-dropping. Frankly, there shouldn’t be, as it is nothing groundbreaking. We’ve had this evolution in wheel size before. So, when I built up the Manzanita and got to riding, I was shocked.

I rode a short route that I frequently ride as a litmus test for gravel bikes. It’s got a bit of everything: paved descents, paved climbs, gravel rail-to-trail, forest service road, rooty single track, and washboard gravel descents. I noticed the behavior of the larger wheels as soon as they touched the first bit of singletrack climb: it carried speed unlike my other bikes. Dips in the trail that might have robbed a bit of speed… didn’t. Roots that would have bounced me off my line… couldn’t. Slick patches that would have required care… I rode through exuberantly. The whole experience felt faster, smoother, and calmer.

Then I hit the washboard descent. Initially I went in with trepidation, like I normally do on this section. Slowly, I let off the brakes until I was flying somewhere north of 40 mph. I could tell I was on a washboard of a road, but the brutal sensation of imminent self-destruct vibration was gone. This was where my jaw almost hit the stem, and not because of a near crash. I was stunned. Washboard at this speed used to feel terrifying, and now it felt tame.

What I Changed

When the Manzanita arrived, it had a 40 mm stem and a setback seatpost. I rode it for a while like this, and eventually changed to a 70 mm stem and a straight seatpost. I preferred the second formula. I don’t like the way that drop bars turn with a short stem. No matter what the headtube angle and fork offset are doing, I much prefer the sensation of turning drop bars with at least a 70 mm stem. Making this change helped me feel more confident and familiar with the front of the bike.

I prefer steeper seat tube angles, and changing the seatpost changed the effective seat tube angle from ~73º to ~74.5º. This change, coupled with a similar change in length to the stem, pushed my whole riding position forward about 20 mm. I noticed a bit more front-end traction, but that might have just been an increase in confidence. The seatpost change also informed a new opinion: you get one kink. If there is a bend in the seat tube, you have to run a straight seatpost. If the seat tube is straight, you can run a setback seatpost. Having two kinks just looks wrong to me. Again, this is simply my opinion on bike aesthetics. I thought the bike looked much better with the straight seatpost.

Climbing

The benefit of the larger wheels was clear pretty quickly. On climbs where the terrain undulates within the wheelbase of the bike, I needed much less effort to maintain momentum. Rocks and roots didn’t bounce me around as much, and it was easier to keep my line. The only downside was that really tight switchbacks felt tighter than on a bike with smaller wheels. This bike is big.

End to end, it’s going to be longer than a bike with an identical wheelbase and smaller wheels. Even with an identical wheelbase to a 29er, there is still 3″ more of total length. I definitely bumped into a tree or two in turns like this and had to get used to the longer bike. I also noticed that initially, these wheels take a bit more effort to start turning – but that is somewhat balanced by their desire to keep turning due to their increase in rotational inertia.

Flat Riding

On flat terrain, I noticed the increase in wheel size the least. This is where it felt most like my other bike. Bellingham’s gravel roads tend to only be rough at steep sections; we don’t have long and flat straights of washboard. I know the bike would have eaten that up while still making it possible to pedal. The first time I remember reading about the concept of big wheels for washboard roads was when Curve announced their Titanosaur project, a 36″ bike that was designed to tame the endless washboard of the Aussie Outback. It made sense then, and to finally feel that difference compared to a 29″ wheel was quite cool.

In Bellingham, we do have a few sections of flat road made of baby-head-sized rocks, but those are frankly so loose and scary that attempting to ride them at any notable speed is terrifying. I’ve had near crashes as a loose rock rolled under my tire on just about every kind of bike I’ve ridden there. Both on this bike and my 29″ bikes, I have to slow down significantly and choose my lines on these uber-rough roads. I’ll get into it more in a bit, but that kind of sums up my feeling on 32″ bikes: yes, these wheels provide a super smooth ride, but they didn’t unlock new terrain or fundamentally change the way I rode a bike.

Descending

Flying down a gravel road and hitting sections of corrugation and undulation was, by far, the scenario in which this bike shined. At high speed and on such a surface, the 32″ wheels made for confidence and composure closer to a mountain bike. My hypothesis is that this larger wheel size, in combination with the speeds achievable by a descending human on a bicycle, interacts “better” with the frequency of road chatter. It’s similar to driving faster on a rough road sometimes feels more comfortable than slowing down and letting the vehicle oscillate through every undulation. I have no way to test this on my own, but I’d love to hear an engineer’s take on it.

On trail, this was also the case. You know how some trailside trees send a network of roots that cascade out of the base of the tree and across the trail surface? It creates a knotty and bumpy hip-like jump on an otherwise flat trail. On a mountain bike, I’ll pop over these. On a gravel bike, I do my best to unweight and glide over the top, but rarely does it feel like I’m going to do so without clanging rim or having some kind of experience that I’ll tell a friend about later. On the 32″ bike, this felt far easier and more pleasant. The bike reacts less as it bounces across the top of the roots instead of wanting to drop into the spaces between them.

The increase in traction was most apparent when cornering. Even on the Teravail Cannonball, a fairly slick gravel tread pattern, I could lean the bike harder than I initially expected. At speed, I was somewhat terrified by the cornering capability of this bike. The traction, though it did end on occasion, was available for far longer and in far greater amounts.

Bad News

The smooth sensation never went away, but here is the bad news: I got used to it. The novelty of the wheel size, much like the bumps it hit, subsided after many rides. You would think that I would turn this into a negative, but quite the opposite: this bike is still a bike. I rode the same trails and gravel roads that I do with all of my other bikes. I wasn’t left with the feeling that I needed to sell those bikes, as they had been rendered obsolete by three more inches of wheel.

On the contrary, riding this bike left me with the realization that the riding experience of every bike is unique and worth appreciating. After all, the bike that I have most enjoyed riding was my friend’s 1980s Specialized Stumpjumper. That bike doesn’t carry the speed that current gravel bikes do. It doesn’t have the capability that current mountain bikes do. It has exactly what that bike has, and it is indescribably special.

The same can be said for the Manzanita. Yes, it’s the smoothest rigid bike I have ever thrown a leg over. I loved every moment of washboard descent, a wild statement. And yet, I never rode a trail that I hadn’t already ridden on my other bikes. I didn’t have more fun or less fun. I’m not sitting here at my desk, thinking, “Wow, I don’t ever want to ride that trail on anything other than a 32″ wheeled bike.”

And yet, I’m going to say that you should seriously consider this wheel size for your next bike. There is no good reason not to do so if you want it.

The Momentum of Innovation

In my Dust Up about the sustainability of the bike industry and how it relates to my life, I wrote about the seemingly unstoppable march towards satisfying more. E-bikes, electronic parts where previously mechanical parts did spectacularly, and mainstream mountain bike culture all tend to rub me the wrong way. Yet I don’t feel that way about 32″ bikes – at least, not yet.

To use the overused and poorly-used acoustic versus electric nomenclature that has become prolific in the discussion of the current state of bicycles: the 32″ bike is, seemingly, the greatest acoustic improvement to the riding experience that I have experienced. It is a smoother ride with zero suspension elements, and that is pretty cool.

I have read both a lot of hate and a lot of love for the incoming large-scale adoption of this new wheel size. My opinion is somewhere down the middle. This Manzanita is a bespoke bike built for one human by another human; it’s not a big corporation “pushing” the sale. Yes, it’s a stunningly smooth ride. I was beyond impressed with how capable and pleasant it was. Am I going to sell all of my bikes to make the switch? No, I like those bikes a lot. They’re great now, and they will be in time as well. Sure, I might consider a 32″ bike, but I don’t feel the need to convert my entire stable of bicycles.

I want to recommend that everybody listen to our podcast episode featuring Daniel Yang as well as read his Dust Up article specifically about 32″ wheels. He discusses how he and the team at Neuhaus Metalworks are starting to design bikes around the 750d tire size, an intermediary size between 32″ and 29″ wheels. This tire size, logically, promises a bit of the advantages of 32″ wheels with less of the disadvantages. Mostly, they are simply easier to fit into a frame and will fit smaller riders.

I really hope that the 32″ wheel helps really tall riders find bikes that ride and look the way they want them to. Do I know that there are more of these bikes coming down the pipeline? Yes, and I’m hoping that the small riders aren’t forgotten and designers don’t abandon the smaller tire sizes.

TL;DR

The Manzanita 32er is a stupendously smooth bike with zero added complexity from suspension elements. It’s an analog wonder. 32″ wheels provide a ride like no other. The traction, the rollover, and the resistance to slowing down all add up to a bike that is capable, confident, and pleasant enough to ride all day. If you like the look, and you have a framebuilder in mind, it’s a concept worth exploring.

Pros

  • Smooth as grease
  • Capable and confident
  • Tall riders who might have struggled to find a bike that fits, please rejoice

Cons

  • Look might be polarizing
  • Few “affordable” 32″ wheeled frames currently available
  • 32″ wheels might not fit smaller riders

This bike will be on display in the Builder Lounge at MADE 2026.
